I have been farming these 6 mu in Quzhou for 35 years. I am 53 now, and while I only finished primary school, I know this land and this climate better than any textbook. My household has three people, but my husband and child both work in factories in town, so except during harvest and planting rush, I manage the day-to-day work alone. Luckily, we have our own well, so I do not worry about water.

This year, I will keep four mu in the wheat-maize double-cropping system that every household around here uses, and I will keep two mu for my stevia. The wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. At the start of this season, I will give it its first spring top-dressing and irrigate when the weather warms up. I always use improved wheat varieties because they resist lodging and disease better than the old types. I will apply about 18 kg of nitrogen, 7 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium per mu for the wheat, irrigating four times total—including the overwintering water and the critical jointing and grain-filling stages. I will spray pesticides three times to control weeds, aphids, and fungus. Before sowing, I use rotary tillage to break up the soil. I expect around 500 kg per mu from the wheat.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will sow hybrid maize on those same four mu. Time is short during that transition, and with limited labor, I will use no-tillage sowing to get the maize in quickly without losing soil moisture. The maize will get about 16 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times—at sowing, at the jointing stage, and during ear filling. Two pesticide applications will be enough, mainly for weeds and corn borer. If the weather is normal, I should harvest about 600 kg per mu.

My other two mu are planted with improved stevia seedlings in the spring. Stevia is picky—it does not like too much nitrogen or the leaves lose sweetness, so I use only about 8 kg nitrogen per mu, but I give it 4 kg phosphorus and 6 kg potassium to keep the stems strong. It needs steady moisture, so I will irrigate four times through the growing season. I have to watch stevia more carefully for insects and mildew, so I will spray three times. I prepare that plot with rotary tillage in early spring. A good year should give me about 300 kg of dried leaves per mu, and the buyer from the processing cooperative pays well for clean, sweet leaves.

This plan keeps my workload manageable with my family away during the week, gives us grain for food and feed, and the stevia brings in the cash we need.
